title: Shutdowns, stone-pelting a thing of past in J&K: LG Sinha
excerpt: Srinagar, Oct 25: Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha on Sunday said the days of shutdowns and stone-pelting in Jammu and Kashmir were over, asserting that the Union Territory was witnessing growing entrepreneurial activity, uninterrupted educational institutions and expanding opportunities for young people. Interacting with participants of Yuva Sangam Phase-VII from educational institutions in Maharashtra, led by IIT Bombay, at Lok Bhavan here, Sinha said Jammu and Kashmir was undergoing a transformation, with new opportunities emerging in tourism, agriculture, technology, handicrafts and education. “Gone are the days of shutdowns and stone-pelting. Today, Jammu Kashmir is making headlines for its thriving startups, with schools, colleges, and businesses operating seamlessly throughout the year,” he said. The Lieutenant Governor said thousands of young entrepreneurs were pursuing new opportunities, while Srinagar and Jammu were witnessing growing theatrical, musical and artistic activities. He urged visiting students to share their experiences of Jammu and Kashmir with their families and friends, saying people-to-people exchanges could help strengthen understanding between different regions. Highlighting the importance of collaboration and mentorship, Sinha said meaningful innovation required cooperation among talented individuals, educational institutions and mentors. He encouraged students to use their knowledge and skills to address practical challenges facing society and develop solutions that could benefit communities. “Partnership is essential in science and technology. Use your knowledge and skills to find solutions to society’s real problems. Consider yourselves ambassadors of national unity, so that every young person can become a bridge-builder who connects society,” he said. Referring to the Ek Bharat Shreshtha Bharat initiative, the Lieutenant Governor said Yuva Sangam was helping strengthen cultural and educational ties among states and Union Territories. He also called upon participating institutions to develop long-term academic partnerships to promote research, innovation and knowledge-sharing. Speaking about emerging technological challenges, Sinha stressed the importance of responsible use of artificial intelligence, particularly in view of growing concerns over misinformation and the ethical implications of new technologies. “Every technological breakthrough brings both immense benefits and disruption. Technology lacks morality and cannot distinguish right from wrong on its own; therefore, human control over Artificial Intelligence is essential,” he said. The Lieutenant Governor urged young people to lead technological transformation while safeguarding democratic values and cultural heritage. He also emphasised sustainable development and encouraged students to remain connected beyond the exchange programme. Principal Secretary to the Lieutenant Governor Govind Jaiswal, NIT Srinagar Registrar Wing Commander Mansi Sunger (Retd), representatives of IIT Bombay, faculty members and students attended the interaction.

title: Maharashtra brothers built an app 'Scrapdeal' that collects 2 lakh kg of scrap/month; hit ₹2.5Cr in FY26
excerpt: Indian households regularly accumulate old newspapers, magazines, cardboard boxes, plastic items, e-waste, metal objects, old clothes, and other materials that are no longer useful to them. Many households dispose of such materials along with regular household waste or leave them for waste collectors, without knowing whether they can be recycled or reused. Although local scrap dealers buy recyclable materials, selling scrap can be inconvenient for people who have to carry it to a shop or wait for a dealer to visit their homes. Pune-based Scrapdeal aims to make recyclable scrap disposal more convenient through its doorstep collection service. Founded in 2019 by Jayesh Pakhale, Ganesh Pakhale, and Vaibhav Pakhale, the company facilitates both B2C and B2B customers to schedule scrap pickups through its app, get their materials weighed at their place, and receive immediate payment. “After collection, Scrapdeal segregates the materials based on their type and sends them to authorised recyclers, paper mills, and metal vendors for further processing, ensuring that recyclable waste is directed towards appropriate recycling channels,” Jayesh Pakhale told Startup Pedia in an exclusive interview. About the Founders of Scrapdeal - Jayesh Pakhale, Ganesh Pakhale & Vaibhav Pakhale Jayesh Pakhale, Ganesh Pakhale, and Vaibhav Pakhale hail from Chalisgaon taluka in Jalgaon district, Maharashtra Jayesh Pakhale, the Founder and CEO, completed his Bachelor of Engineering in Mechanical Engineering from Sinhgad Academy of Engineering, Pune, between 2015 and 2019. His brothers, Ganesh Pakhale, the Co-founder and COO, hold a Bachelor of Science (BSc) degree, while Vaibhav Pakhale, the Co-founder and CFO, holds a Bachelor of Commerce (BCom) degree. Before joining Scrapdeal, Ganesh and Vaibhav were involved in their family's raw cotton trading business in Maharashtra. They joined Jayesh in building Scrapdeal in 2022. Starting a College Project that laid the Foundation for Scrapdeal In 2019, while pursuing his Bachelor of Engineering, Jayesh Pakhale had to vacate his flat during his final year and return it to the owner after cleaning up the waste of around 100 kg that he accumulated. However, he struggled to find a scrap dealer who would come to his doorstep, offer reasonable rates, weigh the materials accurately, and collect everything. In January 2019, when he was in the 7th semester, he decided to address the problem by developing an application through which people could sell scrap as easily as ordering food on Swiggy or Zomato. Jayesh teamed up with some of his friends who had knowledge of coding and IT to develop the application. Initial investment in application development At that time, AI tools were not available to help Jayesh develop the application. With the help of his friends, he designed every screen on paper, including the placement of buttons, search functions, and different categories, before the development work began. The application took almost two to three months to develop, and Jayesh invested around Rs 20,000–25,000 in the development work. By April 2019, the app was ready for use. Getting the First Customers and Starting Scrap Collection After developing the application, Jayesh began reaching out to his college friends and other students who were preparing to vacate their flats. He printed pamphlets, designed them himself, and circulated them through WhatsApp and college groups to attract his first customers. As people started placing requests through the app and over phone calls, Jayesh began collecting scrap using his Activa scooter. “Initially, we did not have any carrier vehicles because we only had our pocket money. There was no investment or anything else. I had my Activa at the time, so I borrowed an electronic weighing scale from my uncle and visited the flats of people who requested a collection,” the Pune-based entrepreneur told Startup Pedia. Initial traction and earnings In the initial days, Jayesh collected around 100–200 kg of scrap on weekdays, with the volume reaching approximately 500 kg per day on weekends. He transported the material using his Activa scooter, often making multiple trips between customers’ flats and his own, which served as a storage space. Jayesh purchased scrap at around Rs 7–8 per kg and sold it for approximately Rs 16 per kg. The business generated around Rs 5,000–7,000 per month, which was enough to cover its operating costs and his personal expenses. COVID-19 Disruption and the restart The business operations of Scrapdeal were severely affected during COVID-19. For around 1.5 years, until early 2022, the business remained non-operational due to government-imposed lockdown restrictions. “With no job, I sold tea and vegetables on the roadside for six to eight months to support myself. My elder brothers, who worked at Bajaj Finance, also helped sustain our household through their salaries,” Jayesh told Startup Pedia. As the lockdown restrictions began to ease, Jayesh approached his brothers, Ganesh and Vaibhav, who agreed to join him. The brothers handed over the backend operations of the application to a professional company and also introduced additional operating models. During that period, they also began organising scrap-collection drives in residential societies. Identifying the Market Gap Post COVID-19 After COVID-19, Jayesh identified a significant gap in the scrap collection market. During the pandemic, the use of electronic devices for work and education increased, contributing to the growing volume of e-waste. Lockdown restrictions also disrupted waste collection in several areas, making it difficult for households to dispose of recyclable materials through conventional channels. Traditionally, people had to call local scrap dealers multiple times to sell old newspapers and other scrap materials or transport them to a dealer's shop themselves. There was also a lack of transparency in pricing, weighing, and the disposal of scrap materials. This was particularly concerning when selling electronic items such as old laptops and CPUs, as customers had limited information about how these materials would be handled or disposed of. Scrapdeal aimed to address these challenges through an online platform that listed the types of scrap it purchased, the rates offered, and information about its disposal process. How does Scrapdeal Work? Scrapdeal follows a doorstep collection process through its mobile application, allowing households and offices to sell their scrap materials without having to visit a local scrap dealer. Step 1: Book a collection Customers download the Scrapdeal application, select a convenient collection date and choose the scrap items they want to sell. They then enter the location from which the scrap needs to be collected. Step 2: Collector assignment and doorstep pickup Once the request is submitted, Scrapdeal assigns it to a collector responsible for that particular area. The collector contacts the customer beforehand and visits their doorstep after receiving confirmation. Step 3: Weighing and payment The collector arrives with an electronic weighing scale and empty bags to collect the materials. The process is cashless and paperless, with payment made immediately through UPI after the customer confirms the amount. Step 4: Segregation and recycling A collector and their vehicle can complete approximately 20 collections in a day. After completing the scheduled pickups, the vehicles return to Scrapdeal's facility, where the collected materials are segregated. The materials are then sent to authorised recyclers and vendors. Current Status: Service Areas, Clients & Pricing Scrapdeal currently serves Pune and the Pune Metropolitan Region, including the Pimpri-Chinchwad (PCMC) area. Alongside its direct-to-consumer (D2C) business, Scrapdeal is also working with B2B clients such as Pune Metro, BG Shirke Construction Technology, Fronuis India, Gronius India, and Elantas Beck. According to Jayesh, Scrapdeal is connected with more than 100 companies in Pune and has over 1,000 D2C customers across the city. The pricing depends on the type of waste. The complete rate card is available on the Scrapdeal application. Current Team & Support System Scrapdeal currently works with more than 100 recycling partners, with different partners handling different types of scrap materials. The company has more than 20 collection vehicles operating daily across its service areas. Its team has also grown to more than 50 people, according to Jayesh. Biggest Milestones and Current Volume Scrapdeal currently collects approximately 200 metric tonnes, or 2 lakh kg, of scrap every month. According to Jayesh, one of Scrapdeal's biggest milestones has been connecting with more than 1 lakh people since starting as a college project in 2019. Annual Revenue Before Ganesh and Vaibhav joined the business, Scrapdeal's annual revenue was approximately Rs 5-6 lakh. In FY 2022-23, the company's revenue reached around Rs 30 lakh, followed by Rs 1.5 crore in FY 2024-25 and Rs 2.5 crore in FY 2025-26. For FY 2026-27, Scrapdeal has projected annual revenue of Rs 5 crore. How Scrapdeal Expanded So Quickly? Scrapdeal initially grew through word-of-mouth marketing without spending on Instagram or Facebook advertisements. Customers shared its flyers in their residential society groups, helping the company reach more people through referrals. For its B2B segment, Scrapdeal acquires clients through direct email outreach, references, and enquiries from companies that discover its online portfolio. FAQ Q. What is Scrapdeal and how does it work? A. Scrapdeal is a Pune-based scrap collection platform founded by Jayesh Pakhale in 2019. Customers can book a doorstep pickup through its application, get their scrap weighed electronically, and receive immediate payment through UPI. Which types of scrap does Scrapdeal collect? Scrapdeal collects paper, plastic, metals, reusable clothes, electronic waste, tyres, and glass bottles. It also handles industrial, construction, office, and institutional scrap. Which cities does Scrapdeal currently serve? According to its founder, Scrapdeal currently serves Pune and the Pimpri-Chinchwad (PCMC) area. The company plans to expand to other metropolitan cities, including Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai and Hyderabad. How much revenue does Scrapdeal generate? Scrapdeal reported revenue of Rs 2.5 crore in FY 2025-26, according to its founder. The company has projected revenue of Rs 5 crore for FY 2026-27.
